personas.name: Priya
personas.profile: Priya, head of product at a 30-person software company. Not technical. She approves releases she cannot really inspect. Arrives from a link a developer sent her, opened on her phone between meetings. She may never scroll past the second screen.

focus.page: Needs to see within ten seconds what problem this solves ("customers saw it before we did"), in her words, not CI words. Leaves when the first screen reads like developer tooling or she has to know what "a check" is.

questions: At 390px, does the first screen say what this is without jargon?
Could she repeat the pitch to her CEO in one sentence?
Does she know what to do next?

personas.name: Marcus
personas.profile: Marcus, a senior frontend engineer who already uses PixelSlash. He reviews pull requests all day and has shipped a CSS change that broke a page nobody looked at. He came in through pixelslash.dev, from Hacker News, GitHub or a colleague, and is often in dark mode at a desktop, sometimes on an iPad.

focus.page: Needs to see a real report, real commands, what runs where, whether it fits his CI, PixelSlash still feeling like itself inside the shared shell, and the rest of the suite visible but optional. Leaves when marketing gloss hides the mechanism, no code appears within a scroll or two, a screenshot looks staged, or the suite crowds out PixelSlash's own navigation.

questions: Is there a command or real output within the first two screens?
Does dark mode look designed, not inverted?
Does PixelSlash still feel like itself inside the shared shell?
Is the way to the rest of the suite visible but optional?
Does the tool switcher make sense without explanation?

personas.name: Sam
personas.profile: Sam, a solo founder or freelancer running a few sites. Careful with money and wary of licences. Arrives from GitHub or a tool page, and wants a working "Try it" and the licence line on the page.

focus.page: Needs to see that it is free to self-host, what the Elastic License 2.0 lets him do, and a working try-it in a few lines. Leaves when the licence is unclear, setup looks heavy, or the tool page reads like a sales page with no command.

questions: Is the licence stated plainly on the tool page?
Does "Try it" work from a copy and paste?
Are "works today" and "planned" clearly kept apart?

personas.name: Dana
personas.profile: Dana, an engineering manager who runs a team of eight and owns the CI budget. Already pays for, or is trialling, a visual testing service. Arrives from a search for an alternative, landing on compare or pricing.

focus.page: Needs to see what it costs, how honest it is about its stage, and what she gives up by switching. Leaves when the stage is hidden or hyped, pricing is vague, or the comparison reads as one-sided.

questions: Can she find the release stage and what it means without hunting?
Does the comparison admit where the other tools win?
Is "paid hosting is planned" clear and not buried?

personas.name: Leo
personas.device: keyboard, 200% zoom, reduced motion, both themes
personas.profile: Leo, a QA lead or engineer who cares about accessibility. Keyboard first, sometimes at 200% zoom, sometimes with reduced motion on. Arrives from anywhere, and judges the brand by whether the site practises what it sells.

focus.page: Needs to see contrast that holds in both themes, visible focus, motion that respects the setting, and no sideways scroll, most of all on the slash demo, the report dialog, the theme toggle and the phone menu. Leaves when a site that sells "see what a change does" has broken focus states or flicker.

questions: Can every control be reached and seen by keyboard?
Does body text keep at least 4.5:1 contrast in Latte and Mocha?
With reduced motion on, does anything still move?
